lesson.title: Décrire une personne: le corps, le physique, le caractère et la famille
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: name the parts of the body with the correct article; describe a person's appearance and character; say who someone is and what they do without relying on dated names; name family members and define family links correctly.
Link to your Week 1 and Week 2 notes: they list body words, sample descriptions and family definitions. Several printed forms there are misspelled or have the wrong article (for example 'le tete', 'la bras', 'le mouton', 'le niveu'). This lesson gives the correct forms. The school notes are kept as they are in their own rows.
1. Le corps (the body). Learn each noun with its article: la tête, les cheveux (masculine plural), le front, les yeux (singular: l'œil), l'oreille (f.), la bouche, le nez, les dents (f.), le cou, la poitrine, la langue, le bras, la main, le doigt, le ventre, le menton (the chin), la cuisse, le pied, le genou, l'épaule (f.), la jambe, l'estomac (m.), la gorge, les lèvres (f.), la joue (the cheek). Careful: le mouton means the sheep, the chin is le menton; the word 'le sien' means 'his/hers' and is not a body part.
2. Le physique. Il est grand. Elle est petite. Il est mince. Elle est de taille moyenne. Il a le nez long. Elle a les cheveux longs (cheveux is masculine plural, so the adjective is longs). Il a le teint clair (light skin tone) / foncé (dark). Elle est charmante. La fille est belle comme sa mère. Tip: describe people kindly and respectfully; avoid words that mock a person's body.
3. Le caractère. gentil / gentille, amical / amicale, aimable, sympa (never changes), intelligent / intelligente, calme, drôle. Il parle lentement (not 'il est parle'). Il ne parle pas beaucoup. Je suis intelligent (a boy speaks) / Je suis intelligente (a girl speaks).
4. La position sociale (what someone does). Qui est le directeur de l'école ? Il s'appelle Monsieur Adeyemi. Il est directeur. Qui est le médecin ? Elle s'appelle Madame Okafor. Elle est médecin. After être a job has no article: Il est professeur. With c'est there is an article: C'est un professeur. Office-holders change, so the names of presidents, governors and pastors printed in older notes are dated; practise with fictional names or check a current list before using a real name.
5. La famille. le grand-père, la grand-mère, le père, la mère, le frère, la sœur, l'oncle, la tante, le cousin, la cousine, le neveu, la nièce, le beau-père, la belle-mère, le beau-frère, la belle-sœur.
Correct definitions: Le père de mon père ou de ma mère est mon grand-père. La mère de mon père ou de ma mère est ma grand-mère. Le père est l'homme qui a un enfant. La mère est la femme qui a un enfant. Le fils de mes parents est mon frère; la fille de mes parents est ma sœur. Le frère de mon père ou de ma mère est mon oncle; la sœur de mon père ou de ma mère est ma tante. Le fils de mon oncle ou de ma tante est mon cousin; sa fille est ma cousine. Le fils de mon frère ou de ma sœur est mon neveu; sa fille est ma nièce. Le frère de mon mari ou de ma femme est mon beau-frère, et le mari de ma sœur aussi. La sœur de mon mari ou de ma femme est ma belle-sœur, et la femme de mon frère aussi.
Note on family words: the notes define beau-frère as 'the son of my beau-père or belle-mère'. That fits only some families (step-relations) and is not the usual meaning. Use a labelled fictional family tree in class instead of assuming every household has the same structure.
Source note: the vocabulary and agreement rules follow standard French reference grammars (see sources); the sentences, names and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Write with the right article: tête, bras, cuisse, oreille, doigt, poitrine.
2. Correct: Le cheveux sont longue. La bras est fort. Il est parle lentement. Le niveu de ma mère.
3. Describe a fictional girl in three sentences (appearance, hair, character).
4. Complete: Le frère de ma mère est mon ___. La fille de ma sœur est ma ___. Le père de mon père est mon ___.
5. Say what the people do: Madame Okafor (médecin), Monsieur Adeyemi (directeur).
6. Draw a short fictional family tree and write four sentences that name relations.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (6 marks): la tête, le bras, la cuisse, l'oreille, le doigt, la poitrine.
2 (4 marks): Les cheveux sont longs. Le bras est fort. Il parle lentement. Le neveu de ma mère (the nephew; the notes' spelling 'niveu' is wrong).
3 (6 marks): 2 for each sentence with correct agreement (for example Elle est grande. Elle a les cheveux courts. Elle est gentille.).
4 (3 marks): oncle; nièce; grand-père.
5 (2 marks): Elle est médecin. Il est directeur.
6 (8 marks): 2 per correct relation sentence; accept any consistent fictional family.
Assessment and feedback: total 29 marks. 25-29 secure; 18-24 developing (redo questions 1 and 2 with the article lists); below 18 reteach with a labelled picture of the body. Pronunciation is judged by the teacher, not by this written task.

lesson.title: Décrire un paysage et un lieu touristique au Nigeria
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: name common landscape features; describe a place with il y a and position words; say where a famous Nigerian place is; write a short description of a landscape.
Link to your Week 3 notes: they list landscape words (la ville, la campagne, la mer, les fleuves, les rivières, la forêt, le désert, la plaine, les montagnes) and a table of tourist places with their states. The notes print 'le foret'; the correct form is la forêt (feminine).
1. Le vocabulaire. la ville (town, city), la campagne (countryside), la mer (sea), le fleuve (a large river that flows into the sea), la rivière (a river that flows into another river), la forêt, le désert, la plaine, la montagne, la colline (hill), le lac (lake), la chute d'eau or la cascade (waterfall), la source (spring), la grotte (cave), le parc national.
2. Où se trouve... ? Position words: au nord, au sud, à l'est, à l'ouest, près de, loin de, entre, au bord de, au pied de, dans l'État de. Say: Olumo Rock se trouve à Abeokuta, dans l'État d'Ogun. Erin Ijesha est une cascade dans l'État d'Osun. Ikogosi est une source d'eau chaude et d'eau froide dans l'État d'Ekiti. Yankari est un parc national dans l'État de Bauchi. Obudu est une station de montagne dans l'État de Cross River. Les grottes d'Ogbunike sont dans l'État d'Anambra. Le lac Tchad est au nord-est du Nigeria, et il est partagé avec d'autres pays.
Note: Zuma Rock is printed in the notes under Abuja; it stands in Niger State, close to Abuja, so say: Zuma Rock est un grand rocher dans l'État du Niger, près d'Abuja.
3. Décrire un paysage avec il y a et c'est: Il y a une rivière, des collines et une grande forêt. C'est un beau paysage. Le village est dans une plaine, entre deux collines. Au nord il y a une forêt; au sud il y a une rivière.
Exemple (original text): Mon village est dans une plaine. Au nord, il y a une grande forêt. À l'est, une rivière traverse le village et les enfants jouent au bord de l'eau. À l'ouest, on voit des collines. Le paysage est très beau, surtout le matin. Je préfère la campagne parce qu'elle est calme.
Source note: the vocabulary follows standard French references (see sources); locations follow Nigerian tourism and state sources already used in the notes; the example text and questions are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Write the article and the English word: forêt, rivière, montagne, désert, mer, plaine.
2. Answer from the example text: Où est le village ? Qu'est-ce qu'il y a au nord ? Où jouent les enfants ? Pourquoi l'auteur préfère-t-il la campagne ?
3. Complete: Olumo Rock se trouve dans l'État d'___. Yankari est dans l'État de ___.
4. Write five sentences describing the landscape near your school or home. Use il y a, près de and au nord/sud/est/ouest.
5. Translate: The waterfall is in Osun State. There are mountains in the east.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (6 marks): la forêt (forest), la rivière (river), la montagne (mountain), le désert (desert), la mer (sea), la plaine (plain).
2 (4 marks): dans une plaine; une grande forêt; au bord de l'eau (au bord de la rivière); parce qu'elle est calme.
3 (2 marks): Ogun; Bauchi.
4 (10 marks): 2 per sentence (1 for correct vocabulary or article, 1 for a correct position word); accept true local description.
5 (4 marks): La cascade est dans l'État d'Osun. Il y a des montagnes à l'est.
Assessment and feedback: total 26 marks. 22-26 secure; 15-21 developing (reread the position words); below 15 reteach with a labelled sketch map. Reading aloud is judged by the teacher.

lesson.title: Ma journée: l'emploi du temps, les jours, les mois et la durée
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: say the days and months correctly; describe a school day and a weekend with times; say how long something has lasted and what has been done since the start of a lesson, a day or a year.
Link to your Week 4 and Week 6 notes: they list the days and months and a daily routine. Corrections: the months are janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre. Septembre is the neuvième month, novembre the onzième and décembre the douzième month (the notes print novembre as douzième and omit décembre). The days are lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche; they do not take capital letters.
1. Ordinal numbers: premier, deuxième, troisième, quatrième, cinquième, sixième, septième, huitième, neuvième, dixième, onzième, douzième.
2. La journée. Je me réveille à cinq heures. Je prie avec ma famille. Je salue mes parents. Je balaie la cour. Je me brosse les dents. Je prends mon bain. Je m'habille. Je prends mon petit déjeuner. Je pars pour l'école à sept heures. J'arrive à l'école à sept heures et demie. Les cours commencent à huit heures vingt et finissent à quinze heures vingt. Je rentre à la maison à seize heures trente. Je déjeune, puis je fais mes devoirs. Je regarde la télévision. Je me couche à vingt-deux heures. Notice: je prends (not je prend), j'arrive (not j'arrives), je me brosse les dents (not je brousse), mes devoirs, à sept heures et demie.
Le week-end: Je me lève à sept heures. Je fais le ménage et la lessive. Je prépare le repas. Je fais la sieste. J'aide ma mère à la cuisine (not 'je m'aider ma mère'). Le soir, nous prions ensemble et je dors à dix heures.
3. Exprimer la durée. depuis + a period or a starting point for something still going on now (present tense): J'étudie le français depuis septembre. Je suis dans cette classe depuis trois ans. pendant + a finished period: J'ai dormi pendant huit heures. de ... à ... / jusqu'à: Les cours durent de huit heures à quinze heures. Je reste à l'école jusqu'à quinze heures vingt. toute la journée: Il pleut toute la journée.
4. Dire ce qu'on a fait depuis le début du cours, de la journée, de l'année. Name the starting point (depuis le début du cours / depuis ce matin / depuis le début de l'année) and use the passé composé for completed actions counted since then: Depuis le début du cours, nous avons lu un texte et nous avons écrit trois phrases. Depuis ce matin, j'ai fait mes devoirs et j'ai aidé ma mère. Depuis le début de l'année, nous avons appris les adjectifs. For a state that is still true use the present: Nous sommes en classe depuis huit heures.
5. Dates nationales importantes (dated facts; check a current calendar): le premier janvier, le jour de l'An; le premier mai, la fête du Travail; le douze juin, la fête de la démocratie; le premier octobre, la fête de l'indépendance; le vingt-cinq décembre, Noël. The Week 2 notes of the next term print 29 mai for democracy; Democracy Day has been observed on 12 June since it was changed from 29 May in 2018. Le vingt-sept mai, la fête des enfants, is observed as Children's Day but is not listed as a public holiday.
Source note: the rules follow standard French grammar references (see sources); sentences and exercises are new. See also SUP-FR-DATES for dates, the clock and depuis, pendant, il y a.
Practice (questions):
1. Write in French: the ninth month; the eleventh month; the twelfth month; the third day of the week.
2. Correct: Je prend mon petit déjeuner. J'arrives à l'école. Je brousse mes dents. Je pries Dieu.
3. Choose depuis, pendant or jusqu'à: (a) J'habite ici ___ cinq ans. (b) J'ai joué ___ une heure. (c) Je reste à l'école ___ quinze heures.
4. Write five sentences about your school day with a time in each.
5. Write two sentences saying what you have done since the start of this lesson.
6. Write in French: 1 October; 12 June; 25 December.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (4 marks): septembre; novembre; décembre; mercredi.
2 (4 marks): Je prends mon petit déjeuner. J'arrive à l'école. Je me brosse les dents. Je prie Dieu (or Je prie avec ma famille).
3 (3 marks): depuis; pendant; jusqu'à.
4 (10 marks): 2 per sentence (1 for a correct verb form, 1 for a correct time expression).
5 (4 marks): 2 per sentence with the passé composé and a depuis start, for example Depuis le début du cours, j'ai écrit deux phrases.
6 (3 marks): le premier octobre; le douze juin; le vingt-cinq décembre.
Assessment and feedback: total 28 marks. 24-28 secure; 17-23 developing (redo question 2 and reread section 4); below 17 reteach with a clock and a calendar. Spoken accuracy is judged by the teacher.

lesson.title: L'accord de l'adjectif: masculin, féminin, singulier et pluriel
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: make an adjective agree in gender and number with the noun it describes; use the special forms (beau, nouveau, vieux, long, gros); correct common mistakes.
Link to your Week 5 notes: they list adjectives with masculine, feminine and plural columns and sample sentences. Several printed entries are wrong (grand/grand, jeun, jaun, vielle, gross, 'les femmes sont charmante', 'le fleur est joli'). This lesson gives the correct table and rules.
Rules. The adjective agrees with the noun, not with the speaker. 1. Feminine: add -e (petit, petite; grand, grande; poli, polie). Adjectives already ending in -e do not change (jeune, jaune, mince, aimable, rapide, solide, sympathique, moderne). 2. Plural: add -s (petits, petites). Adjectives ending in -s or -x do not change in the masculine plural (gros, heureux). 3. Doubling: bon, bonne; gros, grosse; traditionnel, traditionnelle; intelligent, intelligente keeps one n and one t. 4. -eux becomes -euse (heureux, heureuse). 5. -al becomes -aux in the masculine plural (amical, amicaux; amicale, amicales). 6. Special: beau, bel (before a vowel), belle, beaux, belles; nouveau, nouvel, nouvelle, nouveaux, nouvelles; vieux, vieil, vieille, vieux, vieilles; long, longue, longs, longues. 7. Sympa never changes: des filles sympa.
Correct table (masculine singular / feminine singular / masculine plural / feminine plural): petit / petite / petits / petites; joli / jolie / jolis / jolies; grand / grande / grands / grandes; bon / bonne / bons / bonnes; fort / forte / forts / fortes; poli / polie / polis / polies; laid / laide / laids / laides; long / longue / longs / longues; gros / grosse / gros / grosses; heureux / heureuse / heureux / heureuses; beau / belle / beaux / belles; vieux / vieille / vieux / vieilles; amical / amicale / amicaux / amicales.
Corrected sentences: Elle est belle. Elles sont belles. Il est beau. Ils sont beaux. La fille est petite. Les filles sont petites. Elle a les cheveux longs (cheveux is masculine plural). Le bébé est gros. Les bébés sont gros. La femme est charmante. Les femmes sont charmantes. Il est vieux. Ils sont vieux. La couleur est jaune. Les couleurs sont jaunes. Le garçon est aimable. Les garçons sont aimables. La fleur est jolie. Les fleurs sont jolies. Common mistakes: 'le fleur' (fleur is feminine: la fleur); 'elle a les cheveux longue' (cheveux is plural and masculine); 'les bébés sont gross'.
Source note: the rules follow standard French grammar references (see sources); the table has been checked against them; the sentences and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Write the feminine: grand, bon, vieux, beau, heureux, gros.
2. Write the plural: un petit garçon; une jolie fleur; un nouveau livre; un élève amical.
3. Complete with the correct form: Les filles sont (intelligent). La robe est (long). Les chaussures sont (neuf).
4. Correct: Elles ont les cheveux longue. Le fleur est joli. Les femmes sont charmante.
5. Write four sentences describing two fictional people, with correct agreement.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (6 marks): grande, bonne, vieille, belle, heureuse, grosse.
2 (4 marks): de petits garçons; de jolies fleurs; de nouveaux livres; des élèves amicaux.
3 (3 marks): intelligentes; longue; neuves.
4 (3 marks): Elles ont les cheveux longs. La fleur est jolie. Les femmes sont charmantes.
5 (8 marks): 2 per sentence for correct agreement and sense.
Assessment and feedback: total 24 marks. 20-24 secure; 14-19 developing (redo questions 3 and 4 using the table); below 14 reteach with picture cards. Written agreement does not show spoken accuracy.

lesson.title: Grammaire et conjugaison: le présent de partir, se lever, commencer et d'autres verbes
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: conjugate common verbs in the present tense, including partir, reflexive verbs and verbs with spelling changes; complete a text with the right verb forms.
Link to your Week 9 notes: they give a gap-fill text and a conjugation of partir. The notes print 'il par / elle par' (correct: il part, elle part) and translate partir as 'to have' (partir means to leave; to have is avoir). The printed text is also cut off, so a complete model is given below.
1. Regular -er verbs: jouer: je joue, tu joues, il/elle joue, nous jouons, vous jouez, ils/elles jouent. Spelling changes: manger: nous mangeons; commencer: nous commençons. Quitter: je quitte, nous quittons.
2. Partir (to leave): je pars, tu pars, il/elle part, nous partons, vous partez, ils/elles partent.
3. Reflexive verbs have a pronoun: se lever: je me lève, tu te lèves, il/elle se lève, nous nous levons, vous vous levez, ils/elles se lèvent. se coucher: je me couche, nous nous couchons. se dépêcher: je me dépêche, nous nous dépêchons. se retrouver: ils se retrouvent.
4. Être and venir: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont; je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent.
5. Do not add est before an action verb: say il part, not 'il est part'. Do not write the infinitive after the subject: say nous mangeons, not 'nous manger'.
Model text (complete): Tous les jours, mes parents partent au travail à six heures. Mon frère et moi, nous nous levons plus tard parce que nous commençons à huit heures et demie. Nous quittons la maison à huit heures et nous nous dépêchons parce que nous sommes souvent en retard. Le soir, toute la famille se retrouve vers dix-huit heures. Nous mangeons et nous nous couchons vers vingt-deux heures. Quelquefois des amis viennent à la maison, et tous les enfants jouent dans la cour.
Source note: the conjugations follow standard French references (see sources); the model text and exercises are new and complete the cut-off school exercise rather than copying it.
Practice (questions):
1. Conjugate partir for je, tu, il, nous, vous, ils.
2. Complete: Mes parents (partir) à six heures. Nous (se lever) tôt. Nous (commencer) à huit heures. Elle (se dépêcher). Nous (manger) du riz. Ils (venir) demain.
3. Correct: Il par à huit heures. Nous manger du riz. Elle est part.
4. Write three sentences about your family's morning using three different subjects.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (6 marks): je pars, tu pars, il part, nous partons, vous partez, ils partent.
2 (6 marks): partent; nous levons (nous nous levons); commençons; se dépêche; mangeons; viennent.
3 (3 marks): Il part à huit heures. Nous mangeons du riz. Elle part.
4 (6 marks): 2 per sentence for subject-verb agreement and sense.
Assessment and feedback: total 21 marks. 18-21 secure; 12-17 developing (redo question 2 with the tables); below 12 reteach one verb family at a time. Pronunciation of silent endings is judged by the teacher.

lesson.title: Dire son goût, comparer et décrire un objet
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: say what you like and prefer; compare clothes and objects; say what an object is made of and what it is used for.
Link to your Week 7 notes: they give clothing words and sample sentences, and a series 'De quoi sert la table ? La table est un bois'. Several lines need correction: 'un jupe' (une jupe), 'le pantaloon' (le pantalon), 'la robe blanche et plus élégante' (est plus élégante), 'J'aime la couleur vert' (la couleur verte), 'la panier' (le panier), 'la port' (la porte). The questions about material and use were mixed up (see section 3).
1. Dire son goût. J'aime cette robe. J'aime la couleur verte. Je préfère la robe bleue. Je n'aime pas ce pantalon. Qu'est-ce que tu penses de ces lunettes ? Je les trouve jolies. Demonstratives: ce pantalon, cet anorak, cette robe, ces chaussures.
2. Comparer. plus + adjective + que (more ... than), moins + adjective + que (less ... than), aussi + adjective + que (as ... as). La robe verte est moins jolie que la robe blanche. La robe blanche est plus élégante. Cette robe est démodée. Celle-ci me plaît mieux; elle est plus à la mode. The adjective still agrees with the noun: cette jupe est plus longue que l'autre.
Clothes vocabulary: long/longue, court(e), large, léger/légère, grand(e), petit(e), à la mode, démodé(e), une jupe, une robe, un pantalon, des chaussures, des lunettes.
3. Décrire un objet. Two different questions: (a) the material: En quoi est la table ? or De quoi est faite la table ? Answer with en + material: La table est en bois. La chaise est en bois ou en plastique. La porte est en bois. La fenêtre est en verre. Le tableau est en métal. Le ventilateur est en métal et en plastique. Le stylo (le bic) est en plastique. Le panier est en plastique. (b) the use: À quoi sert la table ? La table sert à poser les livres. À quoi sert le ventilateur ? Il sert à rafraîchir la pièce. À quoi sert le tableau ? Il sert à écrire.
Source note: the structures follow standard French references (see sources); the sentences and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Correct: Un jupe verte. Le pantaloon est long. La robe blanche et plus élégante. De quoi sert la table ?
2. Compare two fictional bags with plus ... que and moins ... que, and say which you prefer.
3. Complete: La fenêtre est ___ verre. La table est ___ bois. Le ventilateur sert à ___.
4. Describe one object in your classroom: its material and its use (two sentences).
5. Translate: I prefer this dress. It is more elegant than that dress.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (4 marks): Une jupe verte. Le pantalon est long. La robe blanche est plus élégante. À quoi sert la table ? (or En quoi est la table ?).
2 (4 marks): for example Le sac rouge est plus grand que le sac bleu. Je préfère le sac bleu parce qu'il est plus léger. 1 each for plus ... que, moins ... que, correct agreement, a preference.
3 (3 marks): en; en; rafraîchir la pièce (or refroidir).
4 (4 marks): 2 for the material with en, 2 for the use with sert à.
5 (4 marks): Je préfère cette robe. Elle est plus élégante que l'autre robe.

lesson.title: La composition: Mon école, mon ami(e), ma famille
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: plan and write a short French description of a school and of a person; use the right structures for name, place, size and opinion; revise before handing in.
Link to your Week 8 notes: they give a model composition about a particular school (with a named street, a named head and a pupil count) and a homework list (mon ami, mon père, ma mère, mon professeur de français, mon frère, ma sœur, mon meilleur ami). The model has errors (il ya, beaucop, des professeurs et des étudiants, trios cent). Do not copy real addresses or real names of staff and pupils into shared work; use the fictional model below and write about your own school in general terms.
Plan: 1. Le nom: Mon école s'appelle... 2. Le lieu: Elle est située à... dans l'État de... 3. La taille: C'est une grande école. Il y a environ trois cents élèves. 4. Le type: C'est une école privée/publique, mixte. 5. Les personnes: Le directeur (la directrice) s'appelle... Il/Elle est gentil(le) et sympa. 6. Les sections et les matières: Il y a une section primaire et une section secondaire. Mes matières préférées sont... 7. L'opinion: J'aime mon école parce que... .
Modèle (fictional): Mon école s'appelle le Collège des Palmiers. Elle est située à Ibadan, dans l'État d'Oyo. C'est une grande école privée. Il y a environ trois cents élèves et beaucoup de professeurs. La directrice, Madame Adeyemi, est très gentille. Il y a une section primaire et une section secondaire. Mes matières préférées sont le français et les sciences. J'aime mon école parce que les professeurs sont aimables et les élèves sont sympa.
Corrections: il y a (three words, never 'il ya'); beaucoup de professeurs et d'élèves (after beaucoup use de); des élèves très intelligents (adjective agrees); trois cents (cent takes an s when it is multiplied and not followed by another number: trois cents élèves, but trois cent vingt élèves); chrétienne is feminine for école chrétienne.
Pour décrire une personne: Mon ami(e) s'appelle... Il/Elle a ... ans. Il/Elle est grand(e)/petit(e). Il/Elle a les cheveux courts/longs. Il/Elle est gentil(le) et drôle. Nous jouons ensemble. Je l'aime parce que... .
Source note: the structures follow standard French references (see sources); the model text and tasks are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Correct: Il ya beaucop des professeurs. Mon école est une école chritien. Il y a trios cent élèves.
2. Write eight sentences about your own school (do not use real names of staff): name, place, size, type, two subjects, one opinion.
3. Write six sentences about a friend or family member (a fictional person is acceptable): age, appearance, character, one activity.
4. Reread your work and underline each adjective; check its agreement.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (3 marks): Il y a beaucoup de professeurs. Mon école est une école chrétienne. Il y a trois cents élèves.
2 (16 marks): 2 per sentence (1 for correct structure and spelling, 1 for relevant information).
3 (12 marks): 2 per sentence; check il/elle agreement.
4 (4 marks): 1 for each correctly checked adjective, up to 4.
Assessment and feedback: total 35 marks. 29-35 secure; 21-28 developing (rewrite with the plan); below 21 reteach with the model, sentence by sentence. Give feedback on one correct sentence and one to improve.

lesson.title: Relater un événement passé: le passé composé avec avoir et être
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: form the passé composé correctly with avoir and être; make the participle agree when être is used; tell when, where and for how long something happened; correct the usual mistakes.
Link to your Week 1, Week 5 and Week 6 notes: they conjugate voir, manger, regarder and jouer in the past, turn sentences into the passé composé and give dialogues about a journey and a wedding. Several printed forms are wrong (j'ai manger, j'ai loue, 'Ells ont', 'Moyo a se leve', 'il est revenue'). The correct forms are below.
1. Formation: present of avoir or être + past participle. -er verbs: parler, parlé (manger, mangé; regarder, regardé; jouer, joué; acheter, acheté). -ir verbs: fini, choisi. -re verbs: vendu, entendu, répondu. Common irregular participles: voir, vu; avoir, eu; être, été; faire, fait; prendre, pris; mettre, mis; venir, venu; boire, bu; lire, lu; écrire, écrit.
Voir: j'ai vu, tu as vu, il/elle a vu, nous avons vu, vous avez vu, ils/elles ont vu. Manger: j'ai mangé, tu as mangé, il a mangé, nous avons mangé, vous avez mangé, ils ont mangé. Infinitive and participle are different: j'ai mangé, not 'j'ai manger'.
2. With être: aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir, rester, rentrer, monter, descendre, naître, mourir, and all reflexive verbs. The participle agrees with the subject: elle est allée, ils sont partis, elles sont rentrées, je me suis levé (a boy), je me suis levée (a girl), nous nous sommes levés. Reflexive verbs: the pronoun comes before être; do not write 'a se lever': say Moyo s'est levé très tôt (a boy) or Moyo s'est levée très tôt (a girl).
3. Corrected sentences from your Week 1 exercise: J'ai vu les enfants dans la voiture. Nous avons mangé du riz et de la salade. Kunle a regardé la télévision. Moyo s'est levé très tôt. Wale a acheté une bicyclette. Le match s'est joué à Abuja. Elle s'est dérangée pour rien. Qu'est-ce que vous avez entendu ? Qu'est-ce que les étudiants ont raconté ? Les policiers ont trouvé le bandit. Acheter in the passé composé: j'ai acheté, tu as acheté, il/elle a acheté, nous avons acheté, vous avez acheté, ils/elles ont acheté.
4. Situer l'événement dans le temps: hier, avant-hier, ce matin, la semaine dernière, lundi dernier, il y a deux jours, le 4 avril, du 4 au 15 avril, pendant onze jours. Example report (new): Le 4 avril, Ngozi est partie à Londres pour une conférence. Elle y est restée pendant onze jours. Elle est revenue à Abuja le 15 avril. Elle a visité un musée et elle a acheté des cadeaux. Avant-hier, elle a téléphoné à sa mère.
Note: the notes write 'il est revenue'; for a man it is il est revenu, for a woman elle est revenue. Il y a + period means 'ago' with a past verb: Il est parti il y a deux jours.
Source note: the rules follow standard French grammar references (see sources); the examples and exercises are new, and answers are supplied for the exercises that had none.
Practice (questions):
1. Put into the passé composé: Je regarde un film. Nous mangeons du riz. Elle arrive à huit heures. Ils partent à Abuja. Je me lève à six heures (a girl speaks).
2. Fill the gaps with the right auxiliary (est/sont/a/ont/suis/avons/ai): Tajudeen et Dimeji ___ allés au stade. Ma mère ___ venue chez moi hier. Les enfants ___ pris leur repas. J'___ passé quelques jours à Kano. Ton frère ___ voyagé hier. Nous ___ vu le directeur. Je me ___ levé à six heures (a boy). Ngozi ___ rentrée chez elle.
3. Correct: J'ai manger du riz. Il est revenue hier (a man). Elle a se levé tôt.
4. Write four sentences reporting a real or fictional trip, with two dates or time words.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (5 marks): J'ai regardé un film. Nous avons mangé du riz. Elle est arrivée à huit heures. Ils sont partis à Abuja. Je me suis levée à six heures.
2 (8 marks): sont; est; ont; ai; a; avons; suis; est.
3 (3 marks): J'ai mangé du riz. Il est revenu hier. Elle s'est levée tôt.
4 (8 marks): 2 per sentence (1 for auxiliary and participle, 1 for sense and time expression).
Assessment and feedback: total 24 marks. 20-24 secure; 14-19 developing (redo question 2 using lists of être verbs); below 14 reteach with five verbs at a time. Give feedback on one participle and have the pupil rewrite it.

lesson.title: Rapporter un fait récent: venir de + infinitif et les articles
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: say what has just happened with venir de + infinitive; report a recent fact in a short news item; revise the articles and the contractions au, aux, du, des.
Link to your Week 8 notes: the printed body teaches the articles le, la, l', les and the contractions au, aux (à + le, à + les) and du, des (de + le, de + les), but it does not teach how to report a recent event. Your Week 5 and Week 6 dialogues already contain 'je viens d'arriver de Londres' and 'ma sœur vient de commencer son travail'. This lesson explains that structure. Note: 'aux maisons' means 'to the houses', not 'to the house'.
1. Le passé récent: present of venir + de + infinitive. je viens de, tu viens de, il/elle vient de, nous venons de, vous venez de, ils/elles viennent de. Before a vowel sound: d' (Elle vient d'arriver. Je viens d'écouter la radio.). The second verb stays in the infinitive: Nous venons de finir, not 'nous venons de fini'.
2. Two meanings of venir de: Je viens de Lagos (I come from Lagos: place). Je viens de lire la lettre (I have just read the letter: action).
3. Recent or finished? Use venir de for something that happened a moment ago: La cloche vient de sonner. Use the passé composé with a stated time: Hier, nous avons nettoyé la classe. Do not replace every past tense with venir de.
4. Mots du récit récent: tout à l'heure, il y a un instant, il y a cinq minutes, ce matin, à l'instant, aujourd'hui.
5. Rapporter une nouvelle (original model): Le directeur vient d'annoncer la date de la fête de l'école. Les élèves viennent d'apprendre la nouvelle. Amina vient de recevoir le programme. Nous venons de lire l'annonce. Question: Qui vient d'annoncer la date ? Réponse: Le directeur vient d'annoncer la date.
6. Revision of the articles: le jardin, la porte, l'ami, l'école, les livres. à + le = au (au marché, au cinéma); à + les = aux (aux élèves); à la, à l' do not change (à la bibliothèque, à l'hôtel); de + le = du (le livre du professeur); de + les = des (les livres des élèves).
Source note: the structure follows standard French grammar references (see sources); the news item, sentences and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Complete: Je ___ de terminer mon devoir. Nous ___ d'arriver. Elles ___ de chanter. Vous ___ de lire la lettre.
2. Rewrite with venir de: Il téléphone à sa mère (just now). Les élèves entrent dans la classe (just now).
3. Explain the difference: Je viens de Kano. Je viens de manger.
4. Complete with au, aux, du or des: Je vais ___ marché. Elle parle ___ élèves. Voici le livre ___ professeur. Ce sont les cahiers ___ enfants.
5. Write a three-sentence news item about something that has just happened in school, using three different subjects.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (4 marks): viens; venons; viennent; venez.
2 (2 marks): Il vient de téléphoner à sa mère. Les élèves viennent d'entrer dans la classe.
3 (2 marks): the first is a place (I come from Kano); the second is an action (I have just eaten).
4 (4 marks): au; aux; du; des.
5 (9 marks): 3 per sentence (correct form of venir, de or d' plus infinitive, clear meaning).
Assessment and feedback: total 21 marks. 18-21 secure; 12-17 developing (redo question 1 with the table); below 12 reteach with real events in the classroom. Oral reading is judged by the teacher.

lesson.title: Écrire son journal et une carte postale
lesson.body:
Objectifs / Objectives: write a dated diary entry in the first person; use time words and the passé composé to tell the day in order; write a short postcard to a friend.
Link to your Week 9 notes: they print Bola's report of an excursion and ask for two postcards. The report is a good model. This lesson shows how to plan and check a diary entry and a postcard. A fictional model is used so that no pupil's real day or school details are copied.
1. Le journal (diary): put the date first (Ibadan, le samedi 10 octobre). Write je (the narrator). Say what happened in order with d'abord, puis, ensuite, après, enfin. Use the passé composé for events (je suis allé, j'ai vu) and the imparfait for the scene or feeling (il faisait chaud, j'étais fatigué). End with your reaction: J'ai beaucoup aimé cette journée.
Modèle (fictional): Ibadan, le samedi 10 octobre. Aujourd'hui, je suis allée au marché avec ma mère. D'abord, nous avons acheté du riz et des tomates. Ensuite, j'ai trouvé un joli cahier. Il faisait très chaud et il y avait beaucoup de monde. À midi, nous sommes rentrées à la maison. J'étais fatiguée, mais très contente.
2. Using Bola's report as a guide: it names the day (lundi dernier), the place (Kpalimé), the group (mes amis de l'institut), an event (on a visité le marché), a purchase (j'ai acheté un petit cadeau), an incident (un camion a heurté un arbre), a reaction (il est formidable) and an ending (à la fin de la journée). Check each part when you write your own report.
3. La carte postale: Chère Marie, / Cher Paul, ... Je suis à ... depuis ... Le temps est ... Hier, j'ai visité ... C'était ... Je rentre le ... Amitiés, / Grosses bises, / À bientôt, + your name. Keep a postcard short (four to six sentences).
Modèle: Chère Marie, je suis à Abeokuta avec ma famille. Hier, nous avons visité Olumo Rock. Il faisait beau et la vue était magnifique. J'ai pris beaucoup de photos. À bientôt ! Bola.
4. Check your writing: capital letters only at the start of a sentence and for names; days and months in small letters; participle agreement with être; accents; each sentence has a verb.
Source note: the diary and postcard conventions follow standard French writing guides (see sources); the models and exercises are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Write a diary entry of six sentences about yesterday (real or fictional; say which). Include the date, two times and one feeling.
2. Write two postcards of four sentences each to two friends, describing a trip (you may use details from Bola's report).
3. Correct: lundi dernier, j'ai visité Kpalimé avec tous mes amies. Je suis allé au marché et j'ai acheter un cadeau.
4. Exchange your work with a partner; underline one correct passé composé and one sentence to improve.
Réponses / Answers and marking guide:
1 (12 marks): date 2; ordered events with time words 4; correct auxiliaries and participles 4; a feeling or reaction 2.
2 (12 marks): per postcard: greeting and closing 2; place and activity 2; correct past tense 2.
3 (3 marks): Lundi dernier, j'ai visité Kpalimé avec tous mes amis (amis is masculine plural here). Je suis allé au marché et j'ai acheté un cadeau.
4 (2 marks): the partner names one correct and one improvable sentence with a reason.
Assessment and feedback: total 29 marks. 25-29 secure; 18-24 developing (use the checklist in section 4 and rewrite); below 18 reteach with the model, one paragraph at a time. Give feedback on one verb and have the pupil rewrite that sentence.

lesson.title: Packaging and branding of farm produce
lesson.body:
Objectives: define packaging and branding in agriculture; state the functions of packaging and choose suitable packages for farm produce; list what a good label shows; explain how branding helps a farmer sell.
Link to your notes: Week 2 defines packaging (enclosing and protecting products for distribution, storage, sale and use) and lists advantages and disadvantages. Weeks 3 and 4 define a brand and list four ways companies use branding. The notes are general; this lesson applies them to farm produce in Nigeria.
1. Packaging in agriculture. Packaging contains, protects, preserves, transports, informs and sells a product. For farm produce it reduces bruising, spoilage and loss between farm and market.
Choosing a package (examples): ripe tomatoes and pepper in firm baskets or ventilated crates (soft produce is crushed in sacks); yam tubers in open baskets or stacked with straw (they need air); dry maize, beans and rice in clean, dry bags; garri in sealed polythene or clean sacks (it must stay dry); eggs in trays and cartons; palm oil and groundnut oil in clean sealed containers or bottles; fresh milk and yoghurt in clean closed bottles kept cool; processed products in labelled sachets, jars or tins. A good choice depends on the kind of product, how far it travels, the cost, how long it must keep, what the buyer expects, and the waste left afterwards (choose reusable or recyclable packages where possible).
Disadvantages of packaging (from your notes): it costs money, takes time to design and can slow production. A package that carries an offensive symbol or message can offend a group of people, so use pictures and words that respect everyone.
2. The label. A label tells the buyer what is inside. For a packaged food a label usually shows the name of the product, the producer's name and contact, the quantity (weight or volume), the date of production or best-before date, and how to store it; processed foods also list ingredients. In Nigeria, packaged food is regulated by NAFDAC (the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control), and its Pre-Packaged Food (Labelling) Regulations set what must appear on pre-packaged food labels. A farmer who processes and packs food for sale should check NAFDAC's current requirements before selling. Fresh unprocessed produce sold loose is treated differently from packaged processed food.
3. Branding in agriculture. A brand is a name, words, symbol or design that identifies a product and its maker and sets it apart from competitors. Parts of a brand: brand name, logo (picture or symbol), colours and a short slogan. A brand name can be registered as a trade mark so that others cannot copy it.
How branding helps (your notes list four ways): to market new products, to protect the product's place in the market, to broaden the range of products, and to enter new product categories. In practice it also makes buyers trust quality, helps them find your product again and can allow a fair price for consistent quality.
Worked example: Bisi sells loose garri at 900 naira a measure. She cleans it, seals it in 1 kg polythene packs with a label 'Bisi's Garri' (name, weight, date, her phone number) and a green leaf logo. Customers begin to ask for 'the green-leaf garri', and she can sell a pack at a higher price because quality is steady. Packaging protected the garri, the label informed the buyer, and the brand made it recognisable. (The prices are examples only.)
Packaging, label and brand are different: the package protects, the label informs, the brand identifies.
Source note: the definitions follow the school notes; the Nigerian examples and NAFDAC reference follow NAFDAC and legal-guide sources (see sources). Regulations change, so check the current NAFDAC rules before real sale. The example, questions and answers are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define packaging and branding in agriculture.
2. State four functions of packaging.
3. Choose a suitable package for each and give a reason: tomatoes, garri, eggs, palm oil, yam.
4. List five things a good food label shows.
5. State two disadvantages of packaging and one way to reduce one of them.
6. Design a brand for a fictional farm product: give a name, a logo idea and a slogan, and say how it will help sales.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (4 marks): packaging, the technology of enclosing or protecting products for distribution, storage, sale and use (2); branding, giving a product a name, symbol or design that identifies it and its maker and differentiates it from others (2).
2 (4 marks, one each): any four of contain, protect, preserve, transport, inform, sell.
3 (10 marks, 2 each): tomatoes in firm ventilated baskets or crates to avoid crushing; garri in sealed polythene or clean dry sacks to keep dry; eggs in trays or cartons to prevent breaking; palm oil in clean sealed containers or bottles to avoid spills and contamination; yam in open baskets or stacked with air to prevent rotting. Accept other sensible choices with a reason.
4 (5 marks, one each): any five of product name, producer name and contact, quantity, production or best-before date, storage instructions, ingredients, registration number where required.
5 (3 marks): two of costs money, takes time, can slow production, may offend (1 each); one way to reduce, such as reusing crates or simple standard packs (1).
6 (6 marks): name 2, logo 2, slogan and explanation of how it helps sales 2.
Assessment and feedback: total 32 marks. 27-32 secure; 19-26 developing (redo questions 3 and 4); below 19 reteach with real samples of packaged products. Accept answers in other correct words.

lesson.title: Advertising farm produce: purposes, types and methods
lesson.body:
Objectives: define advertising; state why a farmer advertises; distinguish informative, persuasive and competitive advertising; distinguish direct and indirect methods; choose a sensible and honest way to advertise a farm product.
Link to your notes: Week 5 defines advertising and lists channels (television, radio, print, mail, websites, social media, signs and billboards). Week 6 names informative, competitive and persuasive advertising. Weeks 7 and 8 explain direct and indirect advertisement. This lesson adds farm examples, a way of choosing, and rules of honest advertising.
1. Advertising is controlled communication about a product, usually paid for, meant to make people aware of it and to encourage them to buy. A farmer advertises to inform buyers that the product exists, to make a brand known, to show how the product differs from others, and to increase sales.
2. Types of advertising. Informative: tells buyers about a new product or its benefits. Example: 'New: pawpaw jam from our farm, no added colour, in 250 g jars.' Persuasive: tries to influence the buyer to choose the product. Example: 'Fresh eggs every morning. Taste the difference.' Competitive: claims the product is better than a competing one by direct or indirect comparison. Example: 'Our eggs stay fresh longer than eggs stored for days.' A competitive claim must be true and provable; a false comparison is dishonest advertising.
3. Methods. Direct advertisement speaks straight to the customer and asks for a purchase: text messages or calls to regular customers, a flyer handed out at a market, an email, a stall sign with price, a radio announcement for a market day. Respect customers' consent: do not send unwanted messages repeatedly. Indirect advertisement does not ask for a purchase straight away but makes people aware of the product or the farm by other means: sponsoring a school fair, a free tasting, a farm visit day, appearing in a news story, giving talks, or showing a product in a place people already visit. Indirect advertising builds a relationship; direct advertising asks for the sale.
4. Choosing a channel. Think about who the buyers are, where they are, how much money there is and what message is needed. Illustrative example (figures are for practice): a poultry farmer can choose (a) a roadside banner costing 25,000 naira once, seen by passers-by; (b) a radio announcement costing 40,000 naira a week, heard by many people; (c) messages to 200 regular customers costing about 2,000 naira. If the aim is to keep existing customers, (c) is cheap and direct; to reach new local buyers, (a) is lasting; to reach a wide area quickly, (b) may help but costs more over time.
5. Honest advertising. Say only what is true about the product, its quality and its price. In Nigeria advertising practice is regulated by the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON), under the ARCON Act 2022. Pupils should know that large advertisements are checked by regulators; for a small local farm the rule in class is to be truthful and not to mislead.
Source note: the definitions follow the school notes; the examples and prices are new and illustrative; the regulatory reference is to the ARCON Act 2022 summaries listed in the sources.
Practice (questions):
1. Define advertising and give two reasons a farmer advertises.
2. Name the three types of advertisement and give one farm example of each.
3. Explain the difference between direct and indirect advertising with one example of each.
4. List four channels for advertising farm produce.
5. A farmer sells smoked fish to a nearby town. Suggest one direct and one indirect method and explain your choice.
6. Why must advertising be truthful?
Answers and marking guide:
1 (4 marks): controlled (usually paid) communication about a product to make people aware of it and to encourage buying (2); two reasons such as inform buyers, build brand, show differences, increase sales (2).
2 (6 marks): informative, persuasive, competitive (3); a suitable farm example for each (3).
3 (4 marks): direct speaks to customers and asks for a purchase, for example a text or flyer; indirect creates awareness through other means, such as sponsorship or a free tasting.
4 (4 marks): any four of radio, television, newspapers or magazines, flyers or mail, websites, social media, signs and billboards.
5 (4 marks): a sensible direct method (1) and indirect method (1) and reasons linked to the buyers and cost (2).
6 (3 marks): buyers lose trust and may be misled; false claims can break rules and harm the farm's name; honest claims build lasting customers.
Assessment and feedback: total 25 marks. 21-25 secure; 14-20 developing (redo questions 2 and 5 using the examples); below 14 reteach with real adverts or flyers brought to class. Accept answers in other correct words.

lesson.title: Farm records and bookkeeping: types, uses and a worked example
lesson.body:
Objectives: state why farm records are kept; describe the main types of farm record and what each shows; make simple entries in a cash book and a sales record; calculate profit and a simple inventory.
Link to your notes: Week 2 defines farm records and lists their importance. Week 3 explains bookkeeping (record every transaction daily, with a document for each). Weeks 4 and 5 list seven kinds of record: farm diary, farm inventory, input records, production records, labour records, sales records and consumption records. The notes give the list but no examples. This lesson shows what each record looks like and how it is used.
1. What each record shows (with a sample entry; the figures are for practice).
Farm diary: a day-by-day account of what happens. Example: 12 March, planted maize on 1 hectare, 3 workers, light rain in the evening.
Farm inventory: assets owned and their money value. Example: 2 cutlasses at 5,000 naira each = 10,000; 1 sprayer = 40,000; 1 bag of fertiliser left = 15,000; 2 bags of stored maize at 30,000 = 60,000. Total = 125,000 naira.
Input record: what was put into the farm. Example: seed 60,000; fertiliser (5 bags at 15,000) 75,000; transport 25,000.
Production record: what the farm produced. Example: 20 bags of maize from 1 hectare. It shows which enterprises give the most.
Labour record (labour diary): work done and the cost of labour. Example: 12 March, planting, 3 workers, 1 day each, 2,000 naira each, 6,000 naira in all.
Sales record: what was sold. Example: 20 October, 18 bags of maize at 30,000 = 540,000 naira.
Consumption record: farm produce used by the family. Example: 2 bags of maize kept for the household.
2. Bookkeeping: a simple cash book. Record every receipt (money in) and payment (money out) on the day, with a receipt or note. Example for one maize season: opening cash balance 50,000. Payments: seed 60,000; labour 80,000; fertiliser 75,000; transport 25,000 = 240,000 in total. Receipts: sale of 18 bags at 30,000 = 540,000. Closing cash balance = 50,000 + 540,000 - 240,000 = 350,000 naira.
3. Profit: profit = money received from sales minus costs of production. Here 540,000 - 240,000 = 300,000 naira profit for the season (the opening balance is not profit). If costs were higher than sales, the result would be a loss.
4. Why records matter (from your notes, with meaning): for a correct tax return and tax assessment; to know how much money is coming in and how much can safely be spent; to know profit or loss; to support applications for loans and government assistance; to plan and make a budget; to make good decisions. For example, a production record that shows maize earns more than cassava helps the farmer plan next season.
Source note: the list of records and their importance follow the school notes; the sample entries, cash book and calculations are new, with figures for practice only.
Practice (questions):
1. Define farm records and bookkeeping.
2. List the seven types of farm record in your notes and say what a farm inventory shows.
3. A farmer buys seed for 30,000 naira, pays labour 40,000 and fertiliser 20,000, then sells 10 bags of rice at 15,000 naira a bag. Calculate the total cost, the total sales and the profit or loss.
4. Opening cash is 25,000 naira; receipts are 150,000; payments are 90,000. Find the closing balance.
5. Make a farm inventory for these items: 3 hoes at 2,000 each, 1 wheelbarrow at 20,000, 4 bags of seed at 6,000 each.
6. Explain two ways records help a farmer to get a loan or plan next season.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (4 marks): farm records are written accounts of work, expenses and income in a farm business (2); bookkeeping is recording financial transactions day by day, accurately and with supporting documents (2).
2 (6 marks): farm diary, farm inventory, input records, production records, labour diary, sales records, consumption records (4 for any four named, up to 4 marks); inventory shows assets owned and their money values (2).
3 (4 marks): total cost 30,000 + 40,000 + 20,000 = 90,000 (1); sales 10 x 15,000 = 150,000 (1); profit 150,000 - 90,000 = 60,000 naira (2).
4 (3 marks): 25,000 + 150,000 - 90,000 = 85,000 naira.
5 (4 marks): hoes 6,000; wheelbarrow 20,000; seed 24,000; total 50,000 naira.
6 (4 marks): any two correct reasons with explanation, for example records show lenders the farm earns money; production records show which crop pays best.
Assessment and feedback: total 25 marks. 21-25 secure; 14-20 developing (redo questions 3 and 4 with the worked example); below 14 reteach with a real receipt book. Accept answers in other correct words. These are practice calculations, not advice on real prices.

lesson.title: Importance of the stock exchange and commodity exchange to agriculture
lesson.body:
Objectives: explain what a stock exchange does; explain each reason why it is important to agriculture; distinguish a stock exchange from a commodity exchange; work a simple share example.
Link to your notes: Week 6 defines the stock exchange and lists features and aims. Week 7 names the people involved. Week 8 describes primary and secondary markets. Week 9 lists six reasons it matters to agriculture (capital formation, savings culture, security market, investment opportunity, control of agricultural business, better performance) without explaining them. This lesson explains each.
1. Recap: a stock exchange is an organised market where shares, bonds and other securities are bought and sold. A company that needs money can raise it by selling shares (a share is part ownership of the company). In Nigeria the main exchange is the Nigerian Exchange (NGX), formerly the Nigerian Stock Exchange; the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulates the market.
2. Why it is important to agriculture.
Capital formation: a farm company, such as an oil palm or poultry company, can raise large sums from many investors by selling shares, to buy land, machinery, storage or processing plants.
Savings culture: people with spare money can buy shares or bonds of agricultural companies instead of leaving money idle, which encourages saving and investing.
Security market (a market for securities): shares and bonds can be bought and sold in the secondary market, so an investor can turn them back into cash. This liquidity makes investors more willing to fund farming.
Investment opportunity: investors can put money into agro-allied companies and share in their profits through dividends, and farm businesses can grow with new money.
Control of agricultural business: companies listed on an exchange must follow rules, publish accounts and report regularly. This transparency makes poor management easier to see and protects investors.
Better performance: managers who must report results to shareholders and the market have a reason to run the farm business efficiently.
3. A commodity exchange is different. A stock exchange trades shares and other securities. A commodity exchange trades farm produce such as grains, cocoa or sesame in standard quantities and grades, usually with warehouse receipts that prove produce is stored. Nigeria has private commodity exchange platforms, for example AFEX, a licensed commodity exchange and warehouse-receipt operator. Warehouse receipts can help farmers to get finance and market access. Pupils should check current developments, because markets change.
4. Risks. Share prices can fall as well as rise, so an investor can lose money. A company may pay no dividend in a poor year.
Worked example: a farm company issues 1,000,000 shares at 5 naira each in a public issue. It raises 5,000,000 naira (primary market). Later an investor who bought 2,000 shares sells them to another investor on the exchange (secondary market); the company does not receive that money. If the company pays a dividend of 0.50 naira a share, the investor with 2,000 shares receives 1,000 naira. (The figures are for practice.)
Source note: the six reasons are from the school notes; the explanations, the commodity-exchange comparison and the example are new. NGX and AFEX facts follow the listed sources and should be checked for current details.
Practice (questions):
1. Define a stock exchange.
2. Explain the importance of the stock exchange to agriculture under any four of the six headings in your notes.
3. State two differences between a stock exchange and a commodity exchange.
4. In the worked example, how much does the company raise? How much dividend does an owner of 3,000 shares receive at 0.50 naira a share?
5. Give one risk of buying shares of a farm company.
6. Explain the difference between the primary and the secondary market.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (3 marks): an organised market where shares, bonds and other securities are bought and sold.
2 (8 marks): 2 marks each for the heading and its correct explanation, as in section 2.
3 (4 marks): stock exchange trades shares and securities, commodity exchange trades farm produce in standard grades (2); a commodity exchange uses warehouse receipts or stored produce, a stock exchange uses share certificates or electronic share records (2).
4 (4 marks): 1,000,000 x 5 = 5,000,000 naira (2); 3,000 x 0.50 = 1,500 naira (2).
5 (2 marks): the share price can fall and the investor can lose money, or no dividend may be paid.
6 (4 marks): primary market, newly issued securities sold by the company to investors, so the company gets the money (2); secondary market, existing securities traded between investors, so the company does not get the money (2).
Assessment and feedback: total 25 marks. 21-25 secure; 14-20 developing (redo question 2 with the headings); below 14 reteach with the worked example. Accept answers in other correct words. This is teaching, not financial advice.

lesson.title: Harmful traditional practices: causes, effects, the law and what can be done
lesson.body:
Objectives: define harmful traditional practices; name common examples found in Nigeria and across the world; explain their effects; state what the law and society do about them; correct common wrong ideas about them.
Teacher note: this topic can touch pupils' own lives. Teach it calmly and without blame; do not ask anyone to say what happened in their family. Pupils who are worried about themselves or a friend should be told to speak to a trusted adult such as a teacher, the school counsellor or a parent they trust.
Link to your Week 4 notes: they define harmful traditional practices and list female genital mutilation, slavery, child marriage, widowhood practices, preference for a male child and violence against women, with consequences and preventive measures. This lesson adds corrections and the law.
1. Meaning. A harmful traditional practice is a custom or habit that has been passed down but causes physical, emotional or social harm to a person, usually a woman or a child. 'Traditional' does not make a practice good; every culture keeps what helps people and changes what harms them.
2. Examples. Female genital mutilation or cutting (FGM/C) is the cutting or removal of part of the female genitals for non-medical reasons. It has no health benefit and can cause severe pain, bleeding, infection, long-term health problems, problems in childbirth and lasting fear. Child marriage is the marriage of a person under 18. It often ends education and exposes girls to early pregnancy and its dangers. Harmful widowhood rites are cruel or degrading treatment of widows (forced rituals, isolation, loss of property). Preference for sons leads to the ill-treatment of mothers who have only daughters and to the unequal treatment of girls. Violence against women, including beating, is a crime and not a form of discipline. Trafficking and forced labour are modern forms of slavery and are crimes (see the Week 2 notes on trafficking).
3. Corrections to common wrong ideas. (a) Harmful practices are found in many communities in Nigeria and the world; they should not be blamed on one ethnic or religious group. (b) FGM does not make a girl 'good' or prevent wrong behaviour; there is no evidence that it does. (c) FGM does not 'automatically' cause HIV. The danger is that unsterile or shared cutting instruments can spread infections, including blood-borne infections, so the practice can increase risk; it also has many other harms. (d) The age at which FGM is done differs from place to place, so do not say it is always done on infants. (e) Being a woman or a girl never makes it right to be insulted, beaten or forced.
4. The law (check for your state). The Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015 makes FGM and other violence against persons offences; as a federal law it applies in the Federal Capital Territory and in states that adopt it, so many states have passed their own laws, and pupils should ask which law covers their state. The Child's Rights Act 2003 sets the age of 18 as the age of a child and says that a person under 18 cannot validly marry; it applies in the states that have adopted it. The Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act 2015 deals with trafficking and the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP) enforces it. The Constitution protects the dignity of the person and the right to life (Chapter IV).
5. Consequences (from your notes, with meaning): death, health problems, emotional pain, slowed development (a girl who marries early misses education and growth), and loss of human rights.
6. Prevention. Public enlightenment and school lessons; law and its enforcement; community, religious and traditional leaders who speak against harmful acts; the media; non-governmental organisations; keeping girls in school; help and shelter for victims; changing customs by choice and discussion.
Source note: the list of practices follows the school notes; the corrections and legal references follow World Health Organization and Nigerian law summaries (see sources). Laws can change and states differ, so confirm the current law before quoting it.
Practice (questions):
1. Define a harmful traditional practice.
2. Give four examples and say why each is harmful.
3. Say whether each statement is true or false and explain: (a) Child marriage is practised by only one ethnic group. (b) FGM automatically causes HIV. (c) A custom is good because it is old.
4. Name two Nigerian laws that help protect women and girls and say what each does.
5. Case study: Ada, aged 13, is told she will marry soon. Who can help her and what rights does she have?
6. Give four ways society can reduce harmful traditional practices.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (2 marks): a custom that causes physical or emotional harm, usually to women or children.
2 (8 marks): four examples (4) with a correct reason for each (4).
3 (6 marks, 2 each): (a) false, such practices occur in many communities; (b) false, unsterile instruments can raise the risk of infection but it is not automatic; (c) false, a custom must be judged by whether it harms people.
4 (4 marks): any two correct from the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015, the Child's Rights Act 2003, the trafficking law of 2015, each with its purpose (1 name and 1 purpose).
5 (4 marks): she has a right to education and protection as a child (under 18); she can tell a trusted adult, teacher, counsellor, a relative she trusts, child-protection services or the police.
6 (4 marks, one each): any four from enlightenment, school teaching, law, leaders, media, non-governmental organisations, education for girls, support for victims.
Assessment and feedback: total 28 marks. 24-28 secure; 17-23 developing (redo questions 3 and 4); below 17 reteach calmly with the corrections in section 3. Accept answers in other correct words.

lesson.title: Agriculture in the Nigerian economy: importance, problems and government programmes
lesson.body:
Objectives: place agriculture in the primary sector; explain its importance to the Nigerian economy; state its problems and possible solutions; give the dates of early government agricultural programmes correctly; use a share-of-GDP figure with its date.
Link to your Week 6 notes (Sectors of the Nigerian Economy): they name the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors, then describe agriculture in the primary sector with its importance, problems and solutions. The notes also give dates for early programmes that need correcting. The lesson on the nature of the Nigerian economy (SUP-SS-NATURE-ECONOMY) explains all three sectors with examples; this lesson deepens agriculture.
1. The three sectors. Primary: getting raw materials from nature (farming, fishing, forestry, mining and oil extraction). Secondary: making and building (manufacturing, processing, construction, electricity). Tertiary: services (trade, banking, transport, communication, education, health).
2. Agriculture. Agriculture is the production of crops and animals for food and as raw materials. Importance: food for the people; raw materials for industries (for example cocoa, cotton, oil palm, rubber); jobs for many people, especially in rural areas; export earnings; income for farmers; income for government through taxes; development of rural markets and towns.
3. How big is it? A statistic needs a date. Nigeria's National Bureau of Statistics rebased the national accounts in 2025 (base year 2019). On the rebased figures for 2024, services were about 55.5 per cent of GDP, agriculture about 27.8 per cent and industry about 16.7 per cent (reported by Africa Check, August 2025). Check the latest quarterly report for newer numbers.
4. Problems of agriculture: lack of money or credit; use of simple tools; pests and diseases; poor roads; lack of storage; too few extension workers; inconsistent policy; poor land tenure; low interest of young people; climate and insecurity in some areas. Solutions: loans and support; machines and improved seeds; pest control; roads and storage; extension services; stable policy; training and incentives for youth.
5. Government programmes (corrected dates). Operation Feed the Nation was launched in May 1976 by the military government of General Olusegun Obasanjo to raise food production. The Green Revolution programme replaced it under President Shehu Shagari (1979-83), starting around 1980. A Back to Land programme was carried out under General Muhammadu Buhari's government (1983-85). The notes print 1978 for Operation Feed the Nation and give the Back to Land date and the year of Buhari's government in a confused way; use the dates above. Agriculture remained important until the oil boom of the 1970s changed the economy; crude oil was first found in commercial quantity at Oloibiri in 1956.
6. A skill: reading a share. If agriculture is 27.8 per cent of an economy of 100 units, it is 27.8 units. Compare with services: 55.5 units. Services are about twice agriculture.
Source note: the importance, problems and solutions follow the school notes; dates follow the Central Bank, BusinessDay and Wikipedia accounts listed in the sources, and the GDP shares follow Africa Check citing the National Bureau of Statistics. Historians give slightly different launch details for some programmes, so use 'around' for the Green Revolution.
Practice (questions):
1. Name the three sectors of the economy and give two examples of each.
2. State five ways agriculture helps Nigeria's economy.
3. State four problems of agriculture and a solution to each.
4. Who launched Operation Feed the Nation, and in which year?
5. On the rebased 2024 figures, what share of GDP was agriculture and what share services? Which is bigger and by about how many times?
6. Explain why a statistic must be given with its date.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (6 marks): primary, secondary, tertiary (3) with two correct examples each (3, award 1 per sector).
2 (5 marks, one each): any five of food, raw materials, jobs, export earnings, farmers' income, government revenue, rural development.
3 (8 marks): four problems (4) with matching solutions (4).
4 (2 marks): General Olusegun Obasanjo's military government (1); 1976 (1).
5 (3 marks): agriculture about 27.8 per cent; services about 55.5 per cent; services bigger by about two times (55.5 divided by 27.8 is about 2).
6 (2 marks): figures change with time and with how they are measured (for example rebasing), so an undated figure can mislead.
Assessment and feedback: total 26 marks. 22-26 secure; 15-21 developing (reread sections 2 and 4); below 15 reteach with a local farm example. Accept answers in other correct words.

lesson.title: National security agencies: military, police, DSS and para-military services
lesson.body:
Objectives: define national security; name the main security agencies and state their roles; correct dated details in the notes; state the duties of citizens in security.
Link to your Week 3 and Week 4 notes: they define national security, list citizens' roles, and describe the military, the Nigeria Police, the State Security Service, the Nigeria Immigration Service and the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA). The scheme also names para-military services such as the Civil Defence, which the notes do not cover.
1. National security means the protection of the country, its people and its institutions from threats inside and outside the country.
2. The Armed Forces. Under the 1999 Constitution the Armed Forces are the Army, the Navy and the Air Force. They defend Nigeria from external attack, protect its territory and, when called upon by the President under the law, help to restore order during serious internal disturbances.
3. The Nigeria Police Force. The Constitution provides for one Police Force for Nigeria. It protects lives and property, prevents and detects crime, arrests suspects, keeps law and order and prosecutes cases in the manner the law provides. Proposals for state police are being considered by the National Assembly; a constitution amendment bill covering policing was sent to state assemblies in September 2026 and is not law unless the full amendment process is completed (see the lesson on the constitution).
4. The Department of State Services (DSS). The notes call it the State Security Service (SSS). The SSS was created in 1986 under the National Security Agencies Act (Decree 19) and is widely known today as the Department of State Services (DSS). It deals with domestic intelligence and counter-intelligence, internal security and the protection of the President, Vice-President, governors and other officials.
5. Other agencies. Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC): set up by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps Act 2003 (amended in 2007). Its work includes helping in emergencies and rescue, protecting critical infrastructure such as pipelines and power lines against vandals, and supervising private guard companies. Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS): controls entry and exit of people, issues passports and residence permits (the notes say it was separated from the police in 1958). Nigerian Correctional Service: runs custodial and non-custodial correctional centres under the Nigerian Correctional Service Act 2019. Nigeria Customs Service: collects import and export duties and checks smuggling at borders. National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA): fights the production, trafficking and abuse of illegal drugs; the notes say it was set up by 'Decree 48 of 2000', but the correct date is Decree No. 48 of 1989.
6. Corrections to remember: the insurgency in the north-east was centred on Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states (Maiduguri is the capital of Borno); agencies change names and laws, so check the current name and law.
7. Citizens' duties (from your notes, with meaning): be vigilant and protect public property; report real threats to the police or other security agencies through proper channels; obey the law; show patriotism; and be ready to serve if the law calls on you. Do not take the law into your own hands.
Source note: the citizens' roles and the first five agencies follow the school notes; the corrections and additional agencies follow the NDLEA, Laws of Nigeria and Department of State Services references listed in the sources. Check the current law before quoting any section.
Practice (questions):
1. Define national security.
2. Name the three arms of the Armed Forces and state two roles of the military.
3. State four functions of the Nigeria Police.
4. What was the SSS and what is it commonly called now? Name two of its functions.
5. Name three para-military or other agencies and say what each does.
6. In what year was the NDLEA established, and by what instrument?
7. List four duties of citizens for national security.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (2 marks): protection of the nation and its people from threats inside and outside the country.
2 (4 marks): Army, Navy, Air Force (2); two roles such as defending against external attack, protecting territorial integrity, assisting civil authorities when required by law (2).
3 (4 marks, one each): protect lives and property, prevent and detect crime, arrest suspects, keep law and order, investigate and prosecute.
4 (4 marks): State Security Service (1); Department of State Services (1); two functions such as domestic intelligence, protecting top officials (2).
5 (6 marks): three agencies (3) each with a correct role (3), for example NSCDC protects infrastructure and responds to emergencies; NIS controls entry and issues passports; Customs collects duties and checks smuggling.
6 (2 marks): 1989 (1); Decree No. 48 (1).
7 (4 marks, one each): any four of vigilance, reporting threats properly, obeying laws, patriotism, readiness to serve, protecting public property.
Assessment and feedback: total 26 marks. 22-26 secure; 15-21 developing (redo questions 3 and 5); below 15 reteach by matching agency cards to roles. Accept answers in other correct words.

lesson.title: Self-employment: agencies that help, a business costing and current limits of the notes
lesson.body:
Objectives: state the meaning, forms, needs and sources of funds for self-employment; name agencies that help self-employment and distinguish those that still operate from those only of historical interest; cost a small business and calculate profit.
Link to your Week 5 and Week 6 notes: they define self-employment, list forms (fashion design, catering, photography, carpentry, tailoring and others), the need for self-employment, the sources of funds (savings, gifts, bank loans, ploughed-back profit, government help) and two agencies, NAPEP and the National Directorate of Employment (NDE). This lesson updates the agencies and adds a costing.
1. Recap. Self-employment is working for oneself and earning income from a business one runs personally. It reduces unemployment, develops skills and the economy and raises tax income.
2. Agencies. National Directorate of Employment (NDE): set up under the National Directorate of Employment Act 1989 to fight unemployment through skills training, apprenticeship and loan-linked schemes; your notes list its functions. Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN): a federal agency that supports small and medium businesses with training, information and linkages. Bank of Industry (BOI): a development finance institution that lends to businesses. Microfinance banks: licensed banks that give small loans. National Poverty Eradication Programme (NAPEP): set up in 2001 and described in your notes; it is no longer an operating programme (official statements in 2025 said it had long ceased to exist), so treat it as history. Government schemes change often, so check a current official source or the Ministry before telling someone to apply.
3. Warning about scams. Do not pay money to anyone offering a 'government loan' or job through social media or a website you cannot verify. Check the official government website and ask a trusted adult.
4. Costing a business (figures are for practice). A tailor starts a shop. Start-up costs: sewing machine 120,000 naira; cloth, thread and tools 30,000; shop deposit 50,000. Total start-up = 200,000 naira. Each month: sales 150,000; materials 40,000; rent 20,000; transport and other costs 10,000. Costs = 70,000. Monthly profit = 150,000 - 70,000 = 80,000 naira. Time to recover the start-up money = 200,000 divided by 80,000 = 2.5 months (if sales stay the same). A real plan also allows for slow months, wages and tax.
5. Qualities that help: honesty, skill, saving, good records, good customer care, and willingness to learn.
Source note: the forms, needs and sources of funds follow the school notes; agency descriptions follow the sources listed and should be checked for current status. The costing is a new practice example.
Practice (questions):
1. Define self-employment and give four forms of it.
2. State three needs for self-employment.
3. List five sources of funds for a self-employed person.
4. Name two agencies that help self-employment and say what each does. Which agency in your notes is no longer operating?
5. A baker's start-up costs are 90,000 naira. Monthly sales are 100,000 and monthly costs 60,000. Find the monthly profit and how many months to recover the start-up costs.
6. Why should you check a government scheme at an official source before paying anyone?
Answers and marking guide:
1 (5 marks): working for oneself instead of an employer (1); four forms such as tailoring, catering, photography, carpentry (4, one each).
2 (3 marks): any three of reduces unemployment, develops skills, develops the economy, increases government revenue through tax, speeds economic development.
3 (5 marks, one each): savings, gifts from friends and relatives, bank or microfinance loans, ploughed-back profit, government assistance.
4 (5 marks): two agencies with correct roles (4); NAPEP (1).
5 (4 marks): 100,000 - 60,000 = 40,000 naira a month (2); 90,000 divided by 40,000 = 2.25 months, so about 2 and a quarter months (2).
6 (2 marks): to avoid scams and out-of-date or fake schemes; money paid to a false agent is lost.
Assessment and feedback: total 24 marks. 20-24 secure; 14-19 developing (redo questions 3 to 5); below 14 reteach with a real small business visited or described in class. Accept answers in other correct words.
