lesson.title: Voting, free and fair elections, electoral bodies and electoral malpractice
lesson.body:
Objectives: explain the process of voting; state the conditions for a free and fair election; state correctly the roles of INEC and a State Independent Electoral Commission (SIEC); identify forms and causes of electoral malpractice and ways to prevent them, without party bias.
Link to your Weeks 2 to 7 notes: they teach voter education, voting, the importance of elections and voting, the electoral bodies, free and fair elections and electoral malpractice. Some statements in the notes need correcting or neutral wording (see section 5).
1. Voting. Voting is the act of choosing candidates or deciding an issue. To vote in Nigeria a person must be a citizen aged 18 or over, of sound mind and registered. The voter registers, receives a Permanent Voter's Card (PVC), is checked and accredited at the polling unit, is given a ballot paper, marks it in secret and drops it into the ballot box. INEC uses technology such as the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) to check voters and an online portal to publish polling-unit results. The voters list must be displayed so that errors can be corrected.
2. Free and fair election. Free: every eligible person can register, campaign and vote without fear, force or bribery. Fair: all candidates and parties get equal chances, rules apply equally, votes are counted and results announced honestly. Conditions: an independent and impartial electoral body; an accurate voters register; secret ballot; equal access to the media and public places; peace and security at polling units; honest counting and transparent announcement of results; neutral security agencies; a fair way to settle disputes (election petitions to tribunals and courts); and observers and the media who report what they see.
3. Electoral bodies. INEC is set up by the Constitution. It registers voters and political parties, monitors party conduct, fixes election dates, conducts elections for the President, National Assembly, Governors and State Houses of Assembly, and conducts the area council elections in the Federal Capital Territory; it also educates voters. A State Independent Electoral Commission (SIEC) is created by the Constitution in each state and conducts local government council elections in that state; it also advises INEC on the voters register for those elections. A SIEC has a chairman and between five and seven other members, appointed by the State Governor and confirmed by the State House of Assembly (not appointed by INEC as one of the notes says).
4. Electoral malpractice. Forms: fictitious names on the voters list; separate illegal voters lists; falsifying results; allowing under-age voting; vote buying; ballot box snatching; intimidation of voters, candidates or agents; misuse of state resources; and bias or corruption in handling election disputes. Causes: desire to win at any cost; weak enforcement of the law; poverty that makes vote buying possible; a poor voters register; insecurity; and weak civic education. Ways of preventing it: an independent electoral body; accurate and published registers; strong, impartial security; punishing offenders; civic and voter education; transparent counting and results; and active citizens and observers.
5. Corrections to the notes. (a) INEC does not run local government elections in the states; the SIEC does. (b) INEC does not 'control' parties; it registers them and monitors how they follow the rules. (c) The notes praise or blame named political parties and leaders. A civic lesson judges an election by evidence and rules, not by loyalty to a party: say what happened and what rule was broken or kept. (d) Laws on local government elections and the electoral system are under public discussion, and a 2026 constitution amendment bill covering electoral reform was before state assemblies in September 2026; it is not law until the whole process is completed.
Source note: the voting process and malpractice lists follow the school notes; the legal corrections follow the Constitution as summarised by IDEA and INEC publications (see sources). The examples and questions are new. Check INEC and the Electoral Act for current details.
Practice (questions):
1. State who may vote in Nigeria and describe the steps on election day.
2. Explain 'free' and 'fair' elections and list four conditions for them.
3. State three functions of INEC and two functions of a SIEC.
4. Who appoints a SIEC chairman and members?
5. List four forms of electoral malpractice and two ways of preventing it.
6. Rewrite neutrally: 'The ruling party always rigs elections.' (State a rule or an event instead.)
Answers and marking guide:
1 (5 marks): citizen of 18 or over, of sound mind and registered (2); steps: go to the polling unit, be accredited, receive the ballot paper, vote in secret, drop it in the ballot box (3).
2 (6 marks): free, voters are not forced or afraid (1); fair, equal chances and honest counting (1); four conditions (4).
3 (5 marks): INEC: three of register voters, register and monitor parties, conduct elections for President, National Assembly, Governors and State Assemblies, area council elections in the FCT, voter education (3); SIEC: conducts local government elections and advises INEC on the register (2).
4 (2 marks): the State Governor appoints, subject to confirmation by the State House of Assembly.
5 (6 marks): four forms (4) and two ways of prevention (2).
6 (2 marks): a neutral statement such as 'Observers reported that results at some polling units were changed, which breaks the electoral rules', or any evidence-based wording without party blame.
Assessment and feedback: total 26 marks. 22-26 secure; 15-21 developing (redo questions 3 and 4 with section 3); below 15 reteach by role-playing a polling unit. Accept answers in other correct words.

lesson.title: The 1999 Constitution: sources, features, amendment and the role of citizens
lesson.body:
Objectives: define a constitution; state the sources of the 1999 Constitution; describe its main features; explain how it is amended; explain how citizens contribute to constitutional development.
Link to your Weeks 9 and 10 notes (and the First-Term Week 2 notes on the role of citizens): they define the constitution, name sources, list features and merits and demerits of the 1999 Constitution, and list ways in which citizens help to change the constitution. Some details need correcting.
1. A constitution is the fundamental law of a country. It sets up the government, divides powers and states the rights and duties of citizens. No law or action may go against it (supremacy of the constitution).
2. Sources of the 1999 Constitution. It came into force on 29 May 1999 after the military government issued it as a Decree (the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Promulgation) Decree, No. 24 of 1999). Its text follows the 1979 Constitution closely. The 1979 Constitution introduced the presidential system with the United States as a model, replacing the earlier parliamentary system. Other sources: Nigeria's history and earlier constitutions, customs, traditions and values of the people, and proposals made in constitutional conferences and by leaders and writers (for example Obafemi Awolowo's Path to Nigerian Freedom and Nnamdi Azikiwe's My Odyssey, which shaped political thinking).
3. Features. A preamble that states its purpose; a federal structure of the Federation, 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, with 774 local government areas named in the Constitution; Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy (Chapter II); Fundamental Rights (Chapter IV); separation of powers among the executive, the legislature and the judiciary; a bicameral National Assembly made up of the Senate (109 members) and the House of Representatives (360 members); a multi-party system; a four-year term of office for the President and Governors, limited to two terms; and a rigid process for amendment.
4. Amendment (section 9). An ordinary alteration needs a bill supported by at least two-thirds of all members of each House of the National Assembly and approval by the Houses of Assembly of at least two-thirds of the states (24 of the 36 states), followed by the President's assent. Alterations affecting section 8 (creation of states and local government areas), section 9 itself or Chapter IV (fundamental rights) need at least four-fifths of the members of each House of the National Assembly and the same approval by the state Houses of Assembly. The notes say only 'two-thirds of both houses'; the rest of the process is above. This is why the constitution is called rigid. Status note: a 1999 Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill 2026 covering many areas, including electoral and judicial reform, policing, local government and human rights, was sent to the 36 state Houses of Assembly in September 2026. It is not part of the Constitution unless and until the whole process is completed. Check the latest news.
5. Roles of citizens in constitutional development (from the First-Term notes): voting for representatives who make and amend laws; sending memoranda to the National Assembly; attending public hearings; being nominated or taking part in drafting or reviewing bodies; supporting an independent judiciary that interprets the constitution; peaceful demonstrations and public debate. Institutions that help include the three arms of government, political parties, the electoral commission, civil society, trade unions, the media and student bodies. The armed forces' role is to defend the country under civilian control, not to make constitutions.
6. Merits and criticisms. Merits: protects fundamental rights; separates powers; provides a clear process for amendment; supports stability. Criticisms made by some Nigerians: it began as a military decree and was made without a full popular referendum; it gives much power to the federal government; and it is difficult to amend. Others reply that it has been amended several times through the lawful process. A good answer presents both views and gives evidence.
Source note: features and the amendment procedure follow the Constitution as summarised by legal commentary (see sources); the school notes supply the lists of citizen roles and criticisms; all examples and questions are new.
Practice (questions):
1. Define a constitution.
2. State three sources of the 1999 Constitution.
3. State four features of the 1999 Constitution.
4. Describe the steps for an ordinary amendment, and say what is different for Chapter IV.
5. State four ways in which citizens contribute to constitutional development.
6. Give two criticisms and one merit of the 1999 Constitution.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (2 marks): the fundamental law of a country that sets up government and states rights and duties.
2 (3 marks): any three of the 1979 Constitution, Nigeria's history and earlier constitutions, customs and traditions, conference proposals and writers.
3 (4 marks, one each): any four of preamble, federalism, fundamental rights, separation of powers, bicameral legislature, presidential system, rigidity.
4 (6 marks): two-thirds of all members of each House (2); approval by at least two-thirds of the state Houses of Assembly (2); presidential assent (1); Chapter IV needs four-fifths in each House (1).
5 (4 marks, one each): any four of voting, memoranda, public hearings, nomination or participation in review, independent judiciary, peaceful demonstration.
6 (3 marks): two criticisms (2) and one merit (1).
Assessment and feedback: total 22 marks. 19-22 secure; 13-18 developing (redo question 4 with section 4); below 13 reteach with the process drawn as a flow chart. Accept answers in other correct words.

lesson.title: The nature of the Nigerian economy
lesson.body:
Objectives: define an economy; describe the main features of the Nigerian economy (mixed, developing, dependent on oil for exports and government revenue, with a large informal sector and a service-led output); classify activities into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors; and discuss why diversification matters.
Link to your notes: Week 5 defines the national economy and trade, Week 6 explains the primary sector (agriculture) and mentions that agriculture was the mainstay before large-scale crude oil production, and Week 7 teaches minerals and energy. This lesson describes what kind of economy these activities add up to.
Teaching - what an economy is: an economy is the way a country produces, shares and uses goods and services. 'Nature' means its main features.
1. A mixed economy: private individuals and companies own and run many businesses (farms, shops, factories, banks), while government also owns enterprises, provides services and makes rules. Nigeria is usually described as a mixed economy.
2. A developing, lower-middle-income economy: it is large in total size but income per person is modest and many people still depend on farming, trading and small businesses.
3. Oil dependence: crude oil and gas bring most of Nigeria's export earnings and a large part of government revenue. This does not mean oil is the largest part of national output: after Nigeria's 2025 rebasing of GDP (base year 2019), the 2024 figures show services at about 55.5 per cent, agriculture about 27.8 per cent and industry about 16.7 per cent of GDP, and real estate contributing more than oil and gas (Africa Check, August 2025, citing the National Bureau of Statistics; figures change, so check the latest National Bureau of Statistics report). When oil prices fall, government income and foreign-exchange earnings are affected, which is why depending on one product is risky.
4. A large informal sector: many people work in small, unregistered activities such as market trading, tailoring, roadside food selling and small repairs. Analysts estimate that the informal sector is a very large share of the economy (one commonly quoted estimate is up to 65 per cent), but it is hard to measure because records are cash-based and incomplete.
5. A mix of sectors: primary sector (farming, fishing, forestry, mining and oil extraction); secondary sector (manufacturing, building and construction, processing, electricity); tertiary sector (services such as trade, banking, telecommunications, transport, education and health).
Why diversify: relying on one product exposes a country to price shocks. Strengthening agriculture, manufacturing and services gives more jobs and steadier income.
Worked example: a tailor who buys cloth, makes clothes in a small shop and sells to neighbours without registering is in the secondary (making) and informal parts of the economy; a bank cashier is in the tertiary sector and the formal sector.
Source note: the descriptions follow the sources listed; the examples and questions are new. Percentages are examples from the dates shown, not fixed facts.
Practice (questions):
1. Define an economy.
2. What is a mixed economy? Why is Nigeria described that way?
3. State four features of the nature of the Nigerian economy.
4. Classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary: cassava farming; cement manufacturing; banking; fishing; building a road; telecommunications.
5. What is the informal sector? Give two examples from your area.
6. Explain why depending mainly on oil is risky, and suggest two ways Nigeria can diversify.
Answers and marking guide:
1 (2 marks): the way a country produces, distributes and uses goods and services.
2 (3 marks): an economy in which private and government ownership both operate (2); Nigeria has private businesses and government-owned enterprises and regulation (1).
3 (4 marks, one each): any four of mixed economy; developing or lower-middle-income; oil-dependent exports and revenue; large informal sector; service-led output; mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary activity.
4 (6 marks, one each): cassava farming primary; cement manufacturing secondary; banking tertiary; fishing primary; building a road secondary (construction); telecommunications tertiary.
5 (4 marks): economic activity outside formal registration and records (2); two real examples such as market trading or tailoring (2).
6 (5 marks): price falls reduce government income and foreign exchange (2); any two of strengthening agriculture and food processing, manufacturing, services and technology, solid minerals (1 each); 1 for a clear explanation.
Assessment and feedback: total 24 marks. 20-24 secure; 14-19 developing (reread features 1-5 and redo question 4); below 14 reteach with local examples. Accept answers in other correct words.
